extracted.intended_audience: ML researchers and practitioners evaluating large language model capabilities (engineers, benchmarkers, AI developers)
extracted.subtask_description: Benchmarks and qualitative evaluations for an LLM (GPT-4) on programming (coding-challenges, real-world coding, understanding/executing code, LaTeX, reverse engineering, front-end/game/dev, deep-learning modules) and mathematical problem solving. Includes metrics (pass@k), task designs, and qualitative failure modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proficiency writing focused programs using existing public libraries
rubrics_metrics.description: GPT-4 has a high proficiency in writing focused programs that only depend on existing public libraries, which favorably compares to the average software engineer’s ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a qualitative benchmark: tasks that require combining existing libraries and producing focused functionality; highlights empowerment of both engineers and non-skilled users. Example: writing programs that leverage standard Python/JS libraries or visualization packages. Note caveat: proficiency measured on early GPT-4; definitive numbers may differ on final models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic and semantic correctness of generated code
rubrics_metrics.description: Generated code should be syntactically valid and semantically correct; GPT-4 sometimes produces syntactically invalid or semantically incorrect code, especially for longer or more complex programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both syntax (compilation/interpretation) and semantics (logic, matching specification). Anti-patterns: code that compiles but does not implement intended logic; code with small mistakes that break execution in edge cases. Examples given where GPT-4 occasionally fails on long/complex programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Following instructions and matching intended functionality/style
rubrics_metrics.description: The model should understand and follow user instructions and produce code that matches the intended functionality or stylistic constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess by giving high-level or vague instructions and checking whether the produced code implements requested behaviors and style. Failure modes include misunderstanding vague phrasing or producing code that diverges from requested design. The paper shows GPT-4 can interpret phrases like 'defender avatar is trying to block the enemy' into concrete behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative improvement from human feedback and compiler/terminal errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The model's ability to improve code iteratively when provided human feedback or compiler/terminal errors (e.g., refine a plot; fix compile/runtime errors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation includes multi-turn interactions where user points out errors or requests changes; models should update code accordingly. Examples: iterative refining of a plot; fixing errors flagged by a compiler. Scoring note: ability to interpret error messages and apply appropriate fixes is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmark performance on coding-challenge datasets (HumanEval, LeetCode)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use coding-challenge datasets (e.g., HumanEval's docstring-to-code problems and LeetCode problems) to quantify coding skill, reporting zero-shot pass@1 and pass@5 accuracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metrics: pass@k (whether a correct solution appears in the first k attempts). Control for data leakage by testing on problems posted after pretraining cutoff. Examples: HumanEval (164 problems) and a fresh LeetCode subset; report pass@1 and pass@5 for difficulty bins (easy/median/hard) and overall. Note: compare to other models and human contest performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for memorization/data leakage when benchmarking
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the possibility that the model has seen and memorized benchmark problems during pre-training by selecting fresh/unseen problems (e.g., LeetCode problems posted after the model's pretraining period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct out-of-distribution or post-cutoff test sets to measure generalization. Report separate results for in-distribution and fresh problems. The paper constructs a 100-problem LeetCode benchmark posted after October 8, 2022 to avoid pretraining contamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero-shot vs interactive evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between zero-shot single-prompt generation and interactive/multi-turn evaluation where the model can ask clarifying questions or receive feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report performance for zero-shot (single prompt) settings (e.g., zero-shot pass@1) and consider additional interactive scenarios that may improve outcomes. Examples: zero-shot LeetCode pass@1/pass@5 is reported; some tasks described are interactive (data visualization conversation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-world coding task coverage (domain knowledge, creativity, integration, spec changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate on end-to-end real-world coding tasks that require specialized domain knowledge, creativity, integration across components/libraries, and the ability to modify existing code when the spec changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tasks such as data visualization, LaTeX coding, front-end/game development, and deep learning modules. Criteria include ability to integrate multiple libraries, handle changing specifications, and incorporate domain-specific nuances (e.g., plotting, physics engines, PyTorch internals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data visualization competence (extracting and manipulating data and plotting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to extract data from semi-structured inputs (e.g., LaTeX tables), manipulate into correct formats, produce plots, and respond to follow-up plotting requests (e.g., synchronize y-axis ranges, fix legend duplication, emphasize a particular bar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess correctness of data extraction, formatting, plotting code (e.g., Python plotting libraries), and responsiveness to adjustments. Example: extracting data from Table 2 and producing plots with matching y-axis ranges and legend fixes; distinguishing the 'Human' bar visually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-end and game development capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to interpret very high-level specifications for interactive/front-end or game scenarios and produce functioning code (e.g., 3D HTML game with avatars, physics, obstacles), including implementing implied behaviors (e.g., defender positions itself between player and enemy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate by giving a high-level spec and checking whether the generated application runs and meets requirements: input handling, avatar behavior, physics integration, collision/obstacle logic, trajectory plotting. Example: GPT-4 generated a working 3D game implementing 'body-blocking' defender logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep-learning implementation correctness for custom algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to implement complex custom deep-learning components (e.g., custom optimizer) that require sequence of non-trivial mathematical/data operations (SVD, top-k truncation, normalization by F-norm, percentile truncation, momentum buffers, weight decay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess matching of implementation to a natural-language specification that is intentionally not fully spelled out; check for correct handling of algorithmic details (looping through dimensions, normalization semantics, momentum state buffers). Example: GPT-4 largely matches specified behaviors while a comparator model missed key steps (applying momentum correctly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interfacing with LaTeX and compiling correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert semi-rigorous or buggy LaTeX mixed with natural language into accurate, compiling LaTeX code that preserves intended semantics/formatting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test by providing messy LaTeX-like input and require a one-shot correct compilation-ready LaTeX snippet. Scoring includes syntactic correctness (compiles) and semantic fidelity to the original description. Example: GPT-4 produced a working LaTeX snippet while ChatGPT produced non-compiling output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding and reverse-engineering existing code and binaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to read, interpret and perform reverse engineering on binaries and code: check file format/metadata, disassemble (objdump, radare2), debug (gdb, ltrace), decompile, and reason about algorithms to extract secrets (e.g., password derivation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation includes interactive guidance for running tools, interpreting outputs, suggesting commands, and writing helper scripts to automate brute-force or check hashes. Note ethical/legal considerations: some models may refuse on policy grounds; the paper demonstrates GPT-4 performing penetration-test style reverse engineering in a chat setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoning about platform/compiler specifics (e.g., memory alignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: When predicting outputs of low-level code (C/C++), account for platform/compiler-dependent behaviors such as struct alignment and padding; explain variability and provide example plausible outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume fixed outputs across platforms; explain alignment rules and show example sizes under specific alignment assumptions. Anti-pattern: giving a single numeric answer without discussing compiler/ABI variability (as ChatGPT did).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulated execution of code (Python) with state tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to simulate execution of non-trivial Python code (nested loops, dictionaries, recursion), keep track of intermediate states, and produce the final result with an execution trace in natural language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation: ask for full step-by-step execution of functions (show intermediate dict states, recursion expansion). Correctness judged by whether the simulated trace matches what an interpreter would produce. Example: GPT-4 produced a detailed trace for DP(3,4) and returned the correct value; comparator model did not simulate fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executing and interpreting pseudocode (informal/vague code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret and execute non-strict/informal pseudocode that contains vague or imprecise expressions, including recursive specifications and merge routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment involves giving sketchy pseudocode and asking for the execution trace or final output; judge ability to infer intended semantics and produce a consistent execution (as GPT-4 did for the rec/merge_array example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical problem-solving breadth and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Capabilities include solving difficult (competitive) high-school level math and engaging with advanced topics, but the model can still make basic mistakes and occasionally produce incoherent output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose 'mathematical abilities' into subcomponents (problem formulation, recurrence derivation, algebraic solving, induction reasoning, quantifier handling) and evaluate each separately. Example: GPT-4 solved a 3-year rabbit population recurrence correctly in the example but made occasional imprecise reasoning steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative reasoning and conversational probing in math
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to participate in a mathematical conversation: reformulate problems (function composition perspective), generalize questions (k-fold composition), and respond to follow-ups that probe quantifiers and logical structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate beyond single-answer questions: ask to reformulate, generalize, and detect mis-specified quantifiers. The paper shows GPT-4 largely understands reformulation but can mishandle quantifier nuances in generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental/versioning caveat in reported quantitative results
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative results reported are for an early version of GPT-4 and may differ on the final version; the paper provides numbers for illustration while definitive benchmark results are in the official technical report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using reported metrics, note the model/version used, and treat numbers as illustrative. Benchmarkers should report model snapshots and use fresh test sets to ensure reproducibility.
